solution: $\cos 2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta-1$, so $R_3\to R_3+R_1$ makes the third row $2(\cos^{2}x,\ \cos^{2}2x,\ \cos^{2}3x)$
solution_full: Since $\cos 2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta-1$, the third row is $2(\cos^{2}x,\cos^{2}2x,\cos^{2}3x)-(1,1,1)$, a linear combination of the first row and the row of squares.
Apply $R_3\to R_3+R_1$ (adding a multiple of a row does not change the determinant). The third row becomes $(2\cos^{2}x,\ 2\cos^{2}2x,\ 2\cos^{2}3x)$; take the factor $2$ out.
With $a=\cos x$, $b=\cos 2x$, $c=\cos 3x$ the remaining determinant is the Vandermonde determinant $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\a&b&c\\a^{2}&b^{2}&c^{2}\end{vmatrix}=(b-a)(c-a)(c-b)$.
So $f(x)=2(\cos 2x-\cos x)(\cos 3x-\cos x)(\cos 3x-\cos 2x)$, and $f(x)=0$ exactly when two of $\cos x,\cos 2x,\cos 3x$ are equal.
The value $0$ occurs in all three lists and must be counted once. The distinct zeros are $0,\ \frac{2\pi}{5},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{2\pi}{3},\ \frac{4\pi}{5},\ \pi$.
Hence there are $6$ zeros. Counting $0$ more than once gives $7$ or more; missing the end point $\pi$ gives $5$.
originality_note: New: a Vandermonde determinant hidden by the double-angle relation, whose nodes are cos x, cos 2x, cos 3x, so the zero set is the union of three coincidence sets that overlap (way 5). Closest known: det[[1,1,1],[a,b,c],[a^2,b^2,c^2]] factorisation and counting solutions of cos mx = cos nx. Different because: the Vandermonde form appears only after a row operation, and the count needs the union of three general solutions with a common point.

Checked numerically that f vanishes exactly at the six points and has no other zeros in [0, pi]. Answer 6 at (A) as planned. Changed: No change.
key_step: See the cos 2x row as 2cos^2 - 1, reduce to a Vandermonde determinant, then take the union of three coincidence sets in [0, pi].
justification: Two linked ideas: the hidden Vandermonde form via a row combination, and careful counting over three general-solution families with a shared root and end points. Similar demand to 2025-P2-Q3 (L3), counting trigonometric solutions after a simplification.
